The initial weight of the rotor fixture was 202.46 kg.
Topology optimization resulted in a 16.3% mass reduction for the solid model and a 27.5% mass reduction for the shell model.
The maximum stress value for the original design was 6.9153 MPa, while the new solid body design had a maximum stress of 9.8341 MPa and the new shell body design had a maximum stress of 27.487 MPa.

The maximum deformation for the original design was 0.00251 mm, the new solid body design had a maximum deformation of 0.00275 mm, and the new shell body design had a maximum deformation of 0.00709 mm.
Conventional machining of the rotor fixture had a cost of €9,450 and a lead time of 63 days.
Metal additive manufacturing of the rotor fixture had a 17% higher cost of €11,440 but a 46% reduction in lead time to 34 days.
The rotor fixture was made of 39NiCrMo3 steel, which has a typical yield strength of around 250 MPa.
The mesh quality assessment showed that most elements had a quality between 0.7 and 1, indicating accurate meshing.
The boundary conditions included the rotor fixture flange connected to the compressor casing, bearing loads of 7492 N at the central pad, and 2497 N on each side pad.
60% of the dead weight was applied on the central pad, with 20% each on the side pads.
The axial rotor was 2501 mm long and weighed 2445 kg.
The reaction force on the bearing (Ra) was 11489.8 N, and the reaction force on the rotor fixture (Rb) was 12486.6 N.
The rotor fixture was modeled as a simply supported beam with uniform load.
The topology optimization process aimed to optimize the structural configuration to meet the desired performance objectives, design constraints, and manufacturability requirements.
The final redesigned model was assessed for manufacture using powder bed fusion, a common Selective Laser Additive Manufacturing method.
